Context/Background: To find novel treatments and drug combinations that could effectively target colorectal cancer cells (CRCs) and lower the probability of disease relapse, we designed multiple different combinations between cisplatin, cannabidiol (CBD), and intermittent serum starvation (ISS) on colorectal cancer cell lines. We analyzed differentially expressed genes and affected pathways in colorectal cancer cell lines to understand further the potential molecular mechanisms behind the treatments and their interactions.
Prompt: Based on the results of the differential expression analysis of Cisplatin vs DMSO in colorectal cancer cells, run a pathway overrepresentation analysis for statistically significant genes (up and down combined) against the Reactome database. Then, provide a discussion of any relevant affected pathways, highlighting important up and down regulated genes in each.  Focus on any mechanisms by which Cisplatin may alter cancer related pathways.
output_text:
Introduction/Context  
Differential expression profiling was performed on colorectal cancer (CRC) cell lines treated with cisplatin versus DMSO vehicle. A total of 20,130 genes (Ensembl IDs) were tested; 1,018 genes reached an adjusted p-value (padj)<0.05 and were used for a Reactome over-representation analysis (ORA). Fold-changes ranged from approximately –1.06 to +1.20 (not all shown). No additional assay metadata (e.g., replicates, cell-line names) was specified.

Keywords  
• TP53–mediated cell-cycle arrest  
• Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER) stress / UPR  
• Apoptosis (extrinsic and intrinsic)  
• DNA damage response  
• Metabolic reprogramming  

Candidate Genes  
CDKN1A (p21), GADD45A, DDIT3 (CHOP), BAX, PCNA  

Pathway Enrichments (Reactome ORA on padj<0.05 genes)  

| Pathway                                                                                | Overlap | Adj. p-value       | Leading Genes (examples)                          |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------|--------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| TP53 Regulates Transcription of Cell Cycle Genes                                       | 19/49   | 1.15 × 10⁻⁹        | PLK3; BTG2; CDKN1A; PCNA; GADD45A; BAX             |
| TP53 Regulates Transcription of Genes Involved in G2 Cell Cycle Arrest                 | 8/18    | 3.33 × 10⁻⁴        | PCNA; TFDP1; GADD45A; BAX; SFN; ZNF385A            |
| TP53 Regulates Transcription of Genes Involved in G1 Cell Cycle Arrest                 | 6/14    | 2.70 × 10⁻³        | CDKN1A; CDKN1B; CCNE2; E2F7                        |
| ATF4 Activates Genes in Response to Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress                       | 9/28    | 1.09 × 10⁻³        | DDIT3; ASNS; ATF6; HERPUD1; ATF4                   |
| Response of EIF2AK1 (HRI) to Heme Deficiency                                           | 6/15    | 3.91 × 10⁻³        | EIF2AK1; DDIT3; ATF3; ATF4                         |
| Gluconeogenesis                                                                         | 8/26    | 2.45 × 10⁻³        | GPI; PGK1; ALDOC; ENO1; GAPDH                      |
| PERK Regulates Gene Expression                                                         | 9/33    | 2.41 × 10⁻³        | DDIT3; ASNS; ATF3; HERPUD1; ATF4                   |
| TP53 Regulates Transcription of Cell Death Genes                                       | 11/44   | 1.22 × 10⁻³        | BAX; FAS; PMAIP1; TNFRSF10A/B/C                    |
| Aberrant Regulation of Mitotic G1 S Transition in Cancer Due to RB1 Defects            | 6/17    | 5.44 × 10⁻³        | CDKN1A; CDKN1B; CCND1; CCNE2                       |
| Laminin Interactions                                                                    | 8/30    | 5.02 × 10⁻³        | ITGB4; LAMA3; COL4A5; LAMB1                        |

Analysis  
1. Cell-cycle arrest via TP53: Robust enrichment of “TP53 Regulates Transcription of Cell Cycle Genes” (adj p ~10⁻⁹) and its G1/G2 submodules indicates that cisplatin engages the p53-checkpoint.  CDKN1A (log₂FC = +1.21, padj ≈ 7 × 10⁻²⁵³), GADD45A (+0.41, padj ≈ 1 × 10⁻¹⁰), PCNA, TFDP1 and BAX feature prominently, consistent with DNA damage–triggered arrest and pro-apoptotic signaling.  
2. ER stress / UPR: Enrichment of ATF4- and PERK-driven UPR pathways (adj p ≈ 10⁻³) and “Response of EIF2AK1 to Heme Deficiency” reflects ER stress induction by misfolded‐protein accumulation.  The pro-apoptotic transcription factor DDIT3 (CHOP) is in these sets (DDIT3 log₂FC = –0.43, padj = 0.0038), suggesting translational attenuation and CHOP-mediated apoptosis.  
3. Apoptosis: “TP53 Regulates Transcription of Cell Death Genes” (adj p ≈ 10⁻³) and death-receptor modules (FAS/TNFRSF10A/B/C, PMAIP1) underscore activation of both intrinsic (BAX, BNIP3L) and extrinsic (c-FLIP regulation) apoptosis, matching cisplatin’s known cytotoxic mode.  
4. Metabolic reprogramming: Enrichment for “Gluconeogenesis” (adj p ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻³) highlights shifts in central carbon metabolism, possibly reflecting energy stress downstream of DNA damage.  
5. Extracellular matrix (ECM)/adhesion: The “Laminin Interactions” pathway (adj p ≈ 5 × 10⁻³) and other adhesion modules suggest cisplatin may modulate ECM remodeling or cell–matrix attachment, which could influence migratory/invasive capacity.  

Key Regulators (examples)  
| Gene    | Direction    | Role / Function                       | Pathway(s)                                              |
|---------|--------------|---------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------|
| CDKN1A  | Up (1.21)    | p53-mediated CDK inhibitor; G1 arrest | TP53-Cell Cycle; RB1 G1/S Transition                    |
| GADD45A | Up (0.41)    | DNA damage sensor; G2/M checkpoint    | TP53-Cell Cycle; G2 Arrest                              |
| DDIT3   | Down (–0.43) | CHOP; pro-apoptotic, UPR               | ATF4 / PERK UPR pathways                                |
| BAX     | —            | Mitochondrial apoptosis mediator      | TP53-Cell Death; Cytochrome c release                   |

Implications  
Cisplatin’s cytotoxicity in CRC cells appears driven by canonical p53-checkpoint activation (cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis) and by strong ER stress/UPR engagement leading to CHOP-mediated death. Metabolic reprogramming (gluconeogenesis shift) and ECM remodeling may be secondary adaptive responses.  

Next Steps & Clarifications  
1. Validate p53-dependence by comparing responses in TP53-wildtype versus TP53-null CRC lines.  
2. Measure UPR markers (e.g., BiP/HSPA5, CHOP protein levels) to confirm ER stress.  
3. Assess metabolic flux (e.g., by ^13C-glucose tracing) to verify gluconeogenesis alterations.  
4. Investigate ECM adhesion changes via integrin staining or migration assays.
